stances.claim: Except for portions vested privately under the Torrens System (like the Tirol OCT and its derivatives), the entire island of Boracay is owned by the state.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitive ownership answer distilled from DENR v. Mayor Yap

stances.claim: Prior to Proc 1064, Boracay was unclassified public land treated as public forest under PD 705 -- private parties could not acquire ownership regardless of the length or nature of their possession.
Stripping a forest of its cover (by resorts, restaurants, and commercial establishments) does not convert it from public forest to alienable public land.
Proc 1064 opened the path for Filipinos to apply for judicial confirmation of imperfect titles or other modes of acquiring alienable public land under CA 141.
Duterte can repeal or modify Proc 1064 and reconvert the public lands in Boracay into a protected forest or, better still, a national park that cannot be owned privately.
stances.rhetorical_move: author's prescriptive option for Boracay protection

notable_anecdotes: Tirol OCT No. 19502 (August 7, 1933) -- a pre-constitutional Torrens title issued to the Heirs of Ciriaco S. Tirol as the paradigm example of validly private Boracay land.
The counter-intuitive holding: even beach resorts and restaurants replacing forest cover cannot convert the land from public forest to alienable agricultural land.

The CA 141 two-prong test for judicial confirmation: open/continuous/exclusive/notorious possession from June 12, 1945 AND prior alienable-and-disposable classification -- the second prong was absent in Boracay before Proc 1064.
The author's prescription: national park status would permanently prevent private ownership of Boracay's public lands, a stronger protection than the current alienable-and-disposable classification.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers the question 'Who owns Boracay?' by distilling Secretary of DENR v. Mayor Yap (October 8, 2008), which upheld Proclamation No. 1064 (May 22, 2006) classifying the island into 400 hectares of protected forestland and 628.96 hectares of alienable and disposable agricultural land. Under the Regalian Doctrine -- rooted in Spanish conquest and continued through the 1935, 1973, and 1987 Constitutions -- all land not clearly within private ownership belongs to the state. Only the portions covered by valid Torrens titles, like the 1933 Tirol OCT and its successors-in-interest, are privately owned. Prior to Proc 1064, Boracay was entirely unclassified public land treated as public forest under PD 705, and no one could acquire ownership through possession alone, no matter how long or notorious -- because the essential second prong of the CA 141 judicial-confirmation test (prior alienable-and-disposable classification) was absent. Stripping the forest cover to build beach resorts, restaurants, and commercial establishments does not convert the land from public forest to alienable agricultural land. Proc 1064 changed the status of 628.96 hectares, opening the path for Filipinos to now apply for judicial confirmation of imperfect titles or other modes of acquisition under CA 141. The column closes with the author's own prescription: President Duterte may repeal or modify Proc 1064 and reconvert Boracay's public lands to protected forest, or better still, designate them a national park that cannot be owned privately -- a stronger and more permanent protection.
